claim: Tetrahymena thermophila has seven mating types (I–VII).
source: The model unicellular ciliate, Tetrahymena thermophila, has seven mating types (I–VII).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is supported by citations to previous work (Cervantes et al., 2013; Nanney, 1953; Orias et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2021).

claim: Any cell of one mating type can mate with a cell of any of the other six mating types, but not with one of the same mating type under starvation conditions.
source: Under starvation conditions, any cell of one mating type can mate with a cell of any of the other six mating types, but not with one of the same mating type (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Videos 1–3; Cervantes et al., 2013; Nanney, 1953; Orias et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations and visual evidence from figures and videos.

claim: Mating-type recognition in Tetrahymena depends on direct cell–cell contact.
source: Mating-type recognition in Tetrahymena depends on direct cell–cell contact (temporary or persistent), which suggests that mating-type proteins localize to the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is based on established knowledge about Tetrahymena mating behavior.

claim: When one cell comes into contact with a cell of a different mating type, a mating-type-dependent recognition event enables both cells to enter a pre-conjugation stage called costimulation.
source: When one cell comes into contact with a cell of a different mating type, a mating-type-dependent recognition event enables both cells to enter a pre-conjugation stage (called costimulation) (Bruns and Palestine, 1975; Finley and Bruns, 1980).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Even when cells of different mating types are mixed in unequal ratios (e.g. 9:1), all cells become fully stimulated.
source: Even when cells of different mating types are mixed in unequal ratios (e.g. 9:1), all cells become fully stimulated (Bruns and Palestine, 1975).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: One cell can temporarily contact a number of cells and stimulate them.
source: This is because one cell can temporarily contact a number of cells and stimulate them.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the previous claim about unequal ratio mixing.

claim: Processes that take place during costimulation include Tip transformation and concanavalin A (Con-A) receptor appearance.
source: Processes that take place during costimulation include Tip transformation (Wolfe and Grimes, 1979) and concanavalin A (Con-A) receptor appearance (Figure 1B; Wolfe and Feng, 1988; Wolfe et al., 1986).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations and visual evidence in Figure 1B.

claim: Costimulated cells of the same and different mating type(s) adhere to form very loose pairs.
source: In preparation for pairing, costimulated cells of the same and different mating type(s) adhere to form very loose pairs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Heterotypic cell pairs form a stable conjugation junction, whereas homotypic pairs separate very quickly.
source: Heterotypic cell pairs form a stable conjugation junction, whereas homotypic pairs separate very quickly (Videos 2 and 3; Kitamura et al., 1986).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by video evidence and a citation.

claim: Mating type is determined by a pair of mating-type genes that are organized in head-to-head orientation: MTA and MTB.
source: We previously showed that mating type is determined by a pair of mating-type genes that are organized in head-to-head orientation: MTA and MTB (Figure 1C; Cervantes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation and Figure 1C.

claim: Each mating-type gene has a terminal exon that encodes five transmembrane (TM) helices and a cysteine-rich growth factor receptor (GFR) domain.
source: Each gene has a terminal exon that encodes five transmembrane (TM) helices and a cysteine-rich growth factor receptor (GFR) domain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text describing the gene structure.

claim: The region between the two terminal exons of the gene pair encodes the N-terminal mating-type-specific extracellular regions.
source: The region between the two terminal exons of the gene pair encodes the N-terminal mating-type-specific extracellular regions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: ΔMTB cells do not form pairs or produce progeny.
source: We previously showed that ΔMTB cells do not form pairs or produce progeny and that ΔMTA cells retain mating-type specificity but pair extremely poorly and rarely produced progeny (Cervantes et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ΔMTA cells retain mating-type specificity but pair extremely poorly and rarely produced progeny.
source: We previously showed that ΔMTB cells do not form pairs or produce progeny and that ΔMTA cells retain mating-type specificity but pair extremely poorly and rarely produced progeny (Cervantes et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: The two genes MTA and MTB are non-redundant and both are essential for mating.
source: we concluded that the two genes are non-redundant and both are essential for mating.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous work.

claim: CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 are coexpressed with MTA and MTB and are essential for mating.
source: In addition, our previous work demonstrated that CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 are coexpressed with MTA and MTB and are essential for mating.
evidence: This is stated directly and refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 encoded proteins constitute components of a cyclin-dependent kinase complex, which localizes to the cell tip and pairing junction.
source: These encoded proteins constitute components of a cyclin-dependent kinase complex, which localizes to the cell tip and pairing junction (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: Neither ΔMTA nor ΔMTB can fully transmit/receive mating signal to/from WT cells.
source: However, the experimental results showed that neither ΔMTA nor ΔMTB can fully transmit/receive mating signal to/from WT cells.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rate of pair formation in WT cells pre-incubated with either ΔMTA cells or ΔMTB cells did not increase.
source: To our surprise, the rate of pair formation in WT cells pre-incubated with either ΔMTA cells (Figure 2B, green line) or ΔMTB cells (Figure 2B, blue line) did not increase (i.e. costimulation did not occur).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neither the MTA protein from ΔMTB cells nor the MTB protein from ΔMTA cells can stimulate the WT cell.
source: It indicated that neither the MTA protein from ΔMTB cells nor the MTB protein from ΔMTA cells can stimulate the WT cell, which does not fit any deductions based on the simple receptor–ligand model we proposed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Both MTA and MTB proteins are essential for the mating-type signal.
source: Therefore, both MTA and MTB proteins are essential for the mating-type signal; there is no simple receptor–ligand relationship.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: WT cells were not costimulated even when they were simultaneously incubated with both ΔMTA and ΔMTB cells.
source: In addition, WT cells were not costimulated even when they were simultaneously incubated with both ΔMTA and ΔMTB cells (Figure 2B, teal line)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The absence of a mating-type protein in one cell cannot be complemented by its presence in another cell in the same culture.
source: This result indicates that the absence of a mating-type protein in one cell cannot be complemented by its presence in another cell in the same culture
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental result.

claim: The MTA and MTB proteins must be in the same cell to transmit the mating-type signal.
source: the MTA and MTB proteins must be in the same cell to transmit the mating-type signal.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Mating-type recognition cannot be explained by a simple receptor–ligand model.
source: This finding also suggests that mating-type recognition cannot be explained by a simple receptor–ligand model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: It is possible that the MTA and MTB proteins form a complex which either serves as a recognizer or a co-receptor.
source: It is possible that the MTA and MTB proteins form a complex which either serves as a recognizer (functioning as both ligand and receptor) or a co-receptor.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: It is unlikely that the MTA-MTB complex is acting as a co-receptor because MTA and MTB are the only genes with mating-type specificity.
source: But, since MTA and MTB are the only genes with mating-type specificity, it is unlikely that the complex is acting as a co-receptor.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference based on the genetic data.

claim: During costimulation, cells undergo a sequence of developmental events that remodel the anterior cell membrane and its associated cytoskeleton.
source: During costimulation, cells undergo a sequence of developmental events that remodel the anterior cell membrane and its associated cytoskeleton (Cole, 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: Two hallmarks of costimulation are Tip transformation and Con-A receptor appearance.
source: Two hallmarks of this process are Tip transformation (in which the anterior tip of the cell becomes curved) and Con-A receptor appearance (receptors bound by the plant lectin Con-A, which binds to mannose containing glycoproteins).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: When WT cells of one mating type were mixed with WT cells of another mating type, the cell tips became transformed and Con-A receptors appeared in almost all cells.
source: When WT cells of one mating type were mixed with WT cells of another mating type, the cell tips became transformed (Figure 2C, 4) and Con-A receptors appeared in almost all cells (Figure 2D, 4).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: When WT cells were pre-incubated with ΔMTA, ΔMTB, or both cell types, Tip transformation was not observed in any cell.
source: When WT cells were pre-incubated with ΔMTA, ΔMTB, or both cell types, Tip transformation was not observed in any cell (Figure 2C, 5−7).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: When cells of each mutant were pre-incubated with WT cells, Tip transformation was not detected.
source: Similarly, when cells of each mutant were pre-incubated with WT cells, Tip transformation was not detected (Figure 2C, 8 and 9).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Con-A receptors were not observed in WT cells pre-incubated with ΔMTB cells.
source: Con-A receptors were not observed in WT cells pre-incubated with ΔMTB cells (Figure 2D, 6)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Con-A receptors were not observed in cells of either mutant pre-incubated with WT cells.
source: Con-A receptors were not observed in WT cells pre-incubated with ΔMTB cells (Figure 2D, 6) or in cells of either mutant pre-incubated with WT cells (Figure 2D, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: When WT cells were exposed to ΔMTA or 'ΔMTA cells plus ΔMTB cells', the Con-A receptor was detected.
source: In contrast, when WT cells were exposed to ΔMTA or 'ΔMTA cells plus ΔMTB cells', the Con-A receptor was detected (Figure 2D, 5 and 9)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: ΔMTA cells retain a very weak ability to pair.
source: this is consistent with ΔMTA cells retaining a very weak ability to pair (Cervantes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: Neither ΔMTA and ΔMTB cells can fully stimulate WT cells or be stimulated by WT cells.
source: These results indicate that neither ΔMTA and ΔMTB cells can fully stimulate WT cells or be stimulated by WT cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Costimulation can be separated into two stages: one represented by the appearance of Con-A receptors that only requires MTB protein in partner cells, and the other represented by morphological transformation of the cell tip, which requires both MTA and MTB.
source: They also demonstrate that costimulation can be separated into two stages: (i) one represented by the appearance of Con-A receptors that only requires MTB protein in partner cells, and (ii) the other represented by morphological transformation of the cell tip, which requires both MTA and MTB.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: MTA and MTB cannot functionally complement each other when expressed on different cells.
source: According to the pre-incubation results with 'ΔMTA cells plus ΔMTB cells', MTA and MTB cannot functionally complement each other when expressed on different cells (Figure 2B, teal; Figure 2C, 7).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: ΔCDK19 and ΔCYC9 cells, which express both MTA and MTB, cannot mate.
source: In contrast, we previously found that ΔCDK19 and ΔCYC9 cells, which express both MTA and MTB, cannot mate.
evidence: This is stated directly and refers to previous work.

claim: Pre-incubating WT cells with ΔCDK19 or ΔCYC9 cells of different mating types promotes WT cells mating.
source: Pre-incubating WT cells with each of them of different mating types promotes WT cells mating (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: MTA and MTB proteins form a mating-type recognition complex (MTRC).
source: These findings lead us to propose the hypothesis that MTA and MTB proteins form a mating-type recognition complex (MTRC).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: The MTB protein co-purified with MTA in IP-MS experiments.
source: As expected, the MTB protein co-purified with MTA (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: MRC1–MRC6 proteins co-purified with MTA in IP-MS experiments.
source: As expected, the MTB protein co-purified with MTA (Figure 3B and C), as did another set of proteins, which we named MRC1–MRC6 (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: HA-tagged MTB and MRC1 each pulled down a subset of the proteins that co-purified with MTA.
source: Next, we produced strains expressing either HA-tagged MTB or MRC1 (Figure 3A), and found that each protein pulled down a subset of the proteins that co-purified with MTA (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 3A, 3B, and 3C.

claim: MTA, MTB, and MRC1–MRC6 form the MTRC.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that MTA, MTB, and MRC1–MRC6 form the MTRC.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the IP-MS results.

claim: MTA and MTB may interact with subsets of MRC proteins to form smaller complexes or alternative MTRCs.
source: Alternatively, MTA and MTB may interact with subsets of MRC proteins to form smaller complexes or alternative MTRCs.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: Different protein interactors were identified in extracts from cells at different mating stages.
source: Different protein interactors were identified in extracts from cells at different mating stages.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the IP-MS experiments.

claim: All of the identified components of MTRC are large membrane proteins (predicted size, 92–212 kDa).
source: All the identified components of MTRC are large membrane proteins (predicted size, 92–212 kDa).
evidence: This is stated directly based on the protein analysis.

claim: MRC1 has five predicted TM helices and a GFR domain.
source: Like MTA and MTB, MRC1 has five predicted TM helices and a GFR domain.
evidence: This is stated directly based on domain prediction analysis.

claim: MRC2 has eight TM helices and a pectin lyase-fold domain.
source: MRC2 has eight TM helices and a pectin lyase-fold domain, suggesting a possible role in carbohydrate chain modification.
evidence: This is stated directly based on domain prediction analysis.

claim: MRC3 has two TM helices in the central region and an adjacent ~35 amino acid poly-E region.
source: MRC3 has two TM helices in the central region and an adjacent ~35 amino acid (aa) poly-E region.
evidence: This is stated directly based on protein structure analysis.

claim: MRC4 and MRC5 are both P-type ATPases that are likely to function as calcium-translocators.
source: MRC4 and MRC5 (previously named TPA9; Wang et al., 1997; Wang and Takeyasu, 1997) are both P-type ATPases that are likely to function as calcium-translocators.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations and functional prediction.

claim: MRC6 has four TM helices and a P-loop containing nucleoside triphosphate hydrolases.
source: MRC6 has four TM helices and a P-loop containing nucleoside triphosphate hydrolases.
evidence: This is stated directly based on domain prediction analysis.

claim: Most of the MRC genes are highly coexpressed with MTA and MTB.
source: Most of the MRC genes are highly coexpressed with MTA and MTB (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by expression data in Figure 3E.

claim: Only the sequences of MTA and MTB genes are mating-type-specific.
source: Examination of the whole genome sequences of strains with mating types II–VII confirmed that only the sequences of MTA and MTB genes are mating-type-specific.
evidence: This is stated directly based on genome sequence analysis.

claim: CDK19, CYC9, CIP1, and AKM3 were identified in IP-MS experiments, but with relatively few supporting peptides.
source: In addition to the MRC proteins, CDK19, CYC9, CIP1, and AKM3 were identified in IP-MS experiments, but with relatively few supporting peptides (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 have been proved to be essential for mating.
source: CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 have been proved to be essential for mating (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: AKM3 is predicted to be a K+ channel of unknown biological function.
source: AKM3 is predicted to be a K+ channel of unknown biological function.
evidence: This is stated directly based on functional prediction.

claim: AKM3 is coexpressed with MTA and MTB.
source: It is coexpressed with MTA and MTB (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by expression data in Figure 3E.

claim: The AKM3 deletion strain cannot pair.
source: and we found that the AKM3 deletion strain cannot pair.
evidence: This is stated directly based on experimental observation.

claim: CDK19, CYC9, CIP1, and AKM3 are likely to interact with the mating-type proteins and might be involved in downstream signaling following mating-type recognition.
source: Therefore, these four proteins are also likely to interact with the mating-type proteins (perhaps indirectly and/or via weak interactions) and might be involved in downstream signaling following mating-type recognition.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: MTA7-HA is a membrane protein.
source: Cell fractionation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) revealed that MTA7-HA is a membrane protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: MTA7-HA is exposed on the cell surface.
source: Biotinylation and isolation of cell surface proteins confirmed that MTA7-HA is exposed on the cell surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: MTA7-HA does not localize to the cilia.
source: However, both IP-WB (Figure 4D) and MS (Figure 4—source data 1) consistently failed to identify MTA7-HA protein in the cilia fraction. These results conclusively indicate that MTA7-HA localizes to the cell surface, but not to cilia.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 4D and MS analysis.

claim: MTA7-HA localizes to the cell surface, but not to cilia.
source: These results conclusively indicate that MTA7-HA localizes to the cell surface, but not to cilia.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The MTB2-eGFP strain (which has a mating type VI background) mated normally with WT cells of all mating types except for VI and II.
source: This strain (which has a mating type VI background) mated normally with WT cells of all mating types except for VI and II.
evidence: This is stated directly based on experimental observation.

claim: The overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein is fully functional for mating.
source: This result indicates that the overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein is fully functional for mating.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mating results.

claim: Cells of the MTB2-eGFP strain can mate with one another (self mating).
source: Interestingly, cells of this strain can also mate with one another (self mating)
evidence: This is stated directly based on experimental observation.

claim: A similar selfing phenotype was previously reported for strains expressing multiple mating-type proteins.
source: a similar phenotype was previously reported for strains expressing multiple mating-type proteins (Lin and Yao, 2020).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: The selfing ability of the MTB2-eGFP strain may be caused by the interaction between heterotypic MTRCs.
source: These selfing ability may be caused by the interaction between heterotypic MTRCs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein was detected on the cell surface in a linear pattern radiating from the cell tip to the cell body along the ciliary rows.
source: The overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein was detected on the cell surface in a linear pattern radiating from the cell tip to the cell body along the ciliary rows (Figure 4F, costimulated cell; Figure 4G, mating pair), although signals are also apparent between ciliary rows.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Co-staining with a tubulin dye showed that the MTB2-eGFP protein is adjacent to, rather than co-localizing with, the base of cilia.
source: Co-staining with a tubulin dye showed that the MTB2-eGFP protein is adjacent to, rather than co-localizing with, the base of cilia (Figure 4F and G, enlarged).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: MTB2-eGFP localizes to the cell surface and also to intracellular structures, probably the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, but not to the cilia.
source: Confocal images from the interior of the cell and through the cilia showed that MTB2-eGFP localizes to the cell surface (and also to intracellular structures, probably the endoplasmic reticulum [ER] and Golgi), but not to the cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming our results with the MTA7-HA protein (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MS analysis showed that overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein was not present in isolated cilia of the MTB2-eGFP strain.
source: MS analysis showed that overexpressed MTB2-eGFP protein was not present in isolated cilia of the MTB2-eGFP strain (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by MS data.

claim: Mating-type proteins localize to the cell surface, as might be expected since mating-type recognition depends on cell–cell contact.
source: Therefore, mating-type proteins localize to the cell surface, as might be expected since mating-type recognition depends on cell–cell contact.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion that integrates the localization data with the known requirement for cell-cell contact.

claim: The mating-type-specific region of the MTA and MTB gene pair is the only known genetic locus with mating-type specificity.
source: The mating-type-specific region of the MTA and MTB gene pair is the only known genetic locus with mating-type specificity
evidence: This is stated directly based on genetic analysis.

claim: When WT cells were incubated with MTAxc (and/or MTBxc) of a different mating type, markers of costimulation were not observed.
source: First, we tested whether MTAxc and MTBxc can influence mating in cells with a different mating-type specificity (i.e. non-self-recognition). When WT cells were incubated with MTAxc (and/or MTBxc) of a different mating type, markers of costimulation were not observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treated cells had a significantly increased pairing rate when WT cells were incubated with MTAxc (and/or MTBxc) of a different mating type.
source: Surprisingly, treated cells had a significantly increased pairing rate.
evidence: This is stated directly based on the experimental results.

claim: WT cells pre-treated with MTAxc or MTBxc of different mating types had a similar increased pairing rate.
source: Compared with controls (Figure 5A–C, black), WT cells (VI and VII) pre-treated with MTAxc or MTBxc of different mating types (VII and VI, respectively) had a similar increased pairing rate (Figure 5, green or blue).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Pre-treatment with both MTAxc and MTBxc had a stronger increasing effect on pairing rate than single treatments.
source: It with a stronger increasing effect after pre-treatment with both MTAxc and MTBxc (that is, MTA and MTB have synergistic effect) (Figure 5A–C, teal)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figure 5A-C.

claim: MTA and MTB have synergistic effect on pairing rate.
source: It with a stronger increasing effect after pre-treatment with both MTAxc and MTBxc (that is, MTA and MTB have synergistic effect) (Figure 5A–C, teal), consistent with our finding that MTA and MTB interact with each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data.

claim: Pairing rates increased with increasing MTA6xc and MTB6xc concentrations between 3 pg/ml and 30 pg/ml, with the effect becoming saturated or weaker at higher concentrations.
source: Dose–effect assays showed that pairing rates increased with increasing MTA6xc and MTB6xc concentrations between 3 pg/ml and 30 pg/ml, with the effect becoming saturated or weaker at higher concentrations (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 6A-F.

claim: MTAxc and MTBxc stimulated mating for all other WT mating types.
source: MTAxc and MTBxc also stimulated mating for all other WT mating types (Figure 6G and H), indicating that this is a general effect.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: The mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB proteins are involved in non-self mating-type recognition.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB proteins are involved in non-self mating-type recognition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Treatment of WT cells with MTAxc and/or MTBxc of the same mating type decreased the pairing rate.
source: Treatment of WT cells (VI and VII) with MTAxc and/or MTBxc of the same mating type decreased the pairing rate (Figure 5D and E, green or blue).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: No obvious difference was found between treatments with MTAxc and MTBxc in self-recognition experiments.
source: No obvious difference was found between treatments with MTAxc and MTBxc.
evidence: This is stated directly based on the experimental results.

claim: A significant synergistic effect was observed when WT cells were treated with both MTAxc and MTBxc of the same mating type.
source: Meanwhile, a significant synergistic effect was observed (Figure 5D and E, teal).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: For all treatments (single or combined), the pairing rate was similar by 4 hr (reaching >80%).
source: For all treatments (single or combined), the pairing rate was similar by 4 hr (reaching >80%; Figure 5D and F)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 5D and 5F.

claim: The initial inhibitory effect on pairing by cognate MTAxc and MTBxc was eventually overcome.
source: indicating that the initial inhibitory effect on pairing was eventually overcome.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the time-course data.

claim: Negative regulation by MTAxc and MTBxc was also observed for other mating-type combinations.
source: Negative regulation by MTAxc and MTBxc was also observed for other mating-type combinations (Figure 6I, J).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 6I and 6J.

claim: The mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB proteins mediate both non-self and self recognition.
source: These results support the idea that the mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB proteins mediate both non-self (between different mating types) and self (between the same mating type) recognition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: MTA and MTB form an elaborate multifunctional protein complex that can identify cells of both self and non-self mating types in order to inhibit or activate mating, respectively.
source: Here, we identified a novel MTRC that contains MTA, MTB, and several other proteins and provide evidence that MTA and MTB mediate both self and non-self mating-type recognition (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the study and supported by the experimental data.

claim: T. thermophila uses a dual approach (both self and non-self) to achieve mating-type recognition.
source: indicating that T. thermophila uses a dual approach to achieve mating-type recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Both MTA and MTB proteins are essential for cells to send or receive complete mating-type information.
source: In this study, we found that both proteins are essential for cells to send or receive complete mating-type information
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Transmission of the mating-type signal requires both MTA and MTB proteins to be expressed in the same cell.
source: and transmission of the mating-type signal requires both proteins to be expressed in the same cell.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: MTA and MTB form a mating-type recognition complex that localizes to the plasma membrane, but not to the cilia.
source: We found that MTA and MTB form a mating-type recognition complex that localizes to the plasma membrane, but not to the cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB mediate both self- and non-self-recognition.
source: Stimulation experiments showed that the mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB mediate both self- and non-self-recognition
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Recent research on basidiomycetes and flowering plants has shown that their mating-type recognition mechanisms involve either self- or non-self-recognition.
source: Recent research on basidiomycetes and flowering plants (other species with multiple mating types) has shown that their mating-type recognition (or self-incompatibility) mechanisms involve either self- or non-self-recognition (Fraser and Heitman, 2003; Iwano and Takayama, 2012; Vekemans and Castric, 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: The length of the mating-type-specific region differs significantly among different Tetrahymena species.
source: Our previous evolutionary study showed that the length of the mating-type-specific region differs significantly among different Tetrahymena species (~2000 aa for T. thermophila, ~3200 aa for T. borealis, while only ~1000 aa for T. pigmentosa) (Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by a citation.

claim: Different Tetrahymena species might use different mechanisms for mating-type recognition.
source: Based on the massive difference in length, it is reasonable to speculate that different species might use different mechanisms for mating-type recognition.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the observed differences in mating-type region length.

claim: MTRC is likely to be a giant protein complex which is over a million Daltons in size.
source: MTRC is likely to be a giant protein complex which is over a million Daltons in size.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the sizes of the component proteins.

claim: Mating-type self-recognition might generate an inhibitory signal or might simply inactivate the MTRC.
source: Mating-type self-recognition might generate an inhibitory signal or might simply inactivate the MTRC.

claim: In Papaver rhoeas and Ciona intestinalis, interaction between mating-type proteins of the same mating type induces changes in cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration that cause self-incompatibility.
source: In many species, such as Papaver rhoeas and Ciona intestinalis, interaction between mating-type proteins of the same mating type induces changes in cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration that cause self-incompatibility (Giamarchi et al., 2006; Harada et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: A similar Ca2+-based system may exist in T. thermophila, since the MRC4 and MRC5 proteins are predicted to be Ca2+-translocators.

claim: Interaction between MTRCs on cells of different mating types should result in their activation to allow the cells to initiate pairing.

evidence: This is stated as an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The activation signal involves the CDK19 complex and AKM3.
source: We propose that the activation signal involves the CDK19 complex (a cyclin-dependent kinase complex) (Ma et al., 2020) and AKM3 (a K+ channel; Figure 3C) because they probably interact with the MTRC.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the interaction data.

claim: The MTB2-eGFP cell (VI background) can undergo selfing and mate with cells of all other mating types except VI and II.
source: An intriguing discovery is that the MTB2-eGFP cell (VI background) can undergo selfing and mate with cells of all other mating types except VI and II.

claim: The inability of MTB2-eGFP cells to mate with VI and II supports the self-recognition model.
source: The inability to mate with VI and II supports the self-recognition model.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mating results.

claim: There should be two types of MTRCs in the MTB2-eGFP cell: MTRC of pure VI specificity (A6B6) and heterotypic MTRC of MTA6 and MTB2 (A6B2).

claim: Opposite mating-type recognition outcomes should occur simultaneously when the MTB2-eGFP cell recognizes another MTB2-eGFP cell: inhibition (A6B6–A6B6) and activation (A6B2–A6B2).
source: Consequently, opposite mating-type recognition outcomes should occur simultaneously when the MTB2-eGFP cell recognizes another MTB2-eGFP cell: inhibition (A6B6–A6B6) and activation (A6B2–A6B2).

claim: The selfing ability of the MTB2-eGFP strain indicates there is no or relatively weak inhibitory signal generated during self-recognition.
